title: Design a Logging Framework (Log4j) — Object Model
prompt: Design the object model for a logging framework like Log4j or SLF4J. Application code logs messages at levels (DEBUG/INFO/WARN/ERROR). Messages are filtered by a configured level, formatted, and written to one or more destinations (console, file, network). Design the core classes, the level filtering, the appender/sink abstraction, the formatter abstraction, and how loggers form a hierarchy. Sketch the class diagram.
blurb: Level filtering, pluggable appenders and formatters, and a hierarchical logger tree — the canonical Chain-of-Responsibility OOD.

rubric.label: Requirements clarification
rubric.description: Separates functional (levels, multiple sinks, formatting, hierarchy, config) from non-functional (low overhead when disabled, thread-safe, extensible sinks).

rubric.label: Core entities
rubric.description: Logger, LogLevel, LogRecord/LogEvent, Appender/Sink, Formatter/Layout, Filter, LoggerConfig — cleanly separated.

rubric.label: Class design & responsibilities
rubric.description: Logger decides whether to log; Appender decides where; Formatter decides how it looks; Filter decides fine-grained inclusion. SRP throughout.

rubric.label: Relationships & cardinality
rubric.description: Logger 1..* Appender; Appender 1 Formatter; Loggers form a parent/child tree with level inheritance and appender additivity.

rubric.label: Design patterns
rubric.description: Chain of Responsibility for the logger hierarchy / filter chain, Strategy for Formatter, composition for Appenders, Factory/Singleton for LoggerFactory, optional Observer.

rubric.label: SOLID / OCP
rubric.description: New appender (Kafka) or formatter (JSON) plugs in without editing Logger; level check gates work early (perf).

rubric.label: API / method design
rubric.description: logger.debug/info/warn/error, isEnabled(level), addAppender, setLevel, format(record) — clear signatures.

rubric.label: Extensibility
rubric.description: New sinks/formatters/filters, async logging, structured logging, MDC/context added without core rewrites.

rubric.label: Edge cases
rubric.description: Level below threshold (skip cheaply), appender I/O failure isolation, expensive-argument evaluation, recursive logging, config reload.

rubric.label: Concurrency & performance
rubric.description: Thread-safe writes to a shared file/console, async queue + backpressure, avoiding lock contention on the hot path.

rubric.label: Communication
rubric.description: Narrates the logger hierarchy and appender pipeline, states tradeoffs, reasons about the disabled-log fast path.

functional_requirements: Log messages at levels DEBUG < INFO < WARN < ERROR (and OFF/ALL boundaries)
Filter out messages below the logger's configured threshold cheaply
Write each accepted message to one or more appenders (console, file, network)
Format the message via a configurable layout (plain, pattern, JSON)
Named loggers form a hierarchy with level inheritance and appender additivity
nonfunctional_requirements: Near-zero cost when a level is disabled (fast guard before doing work)
Thread-safe: many threads log to the same appender concurrently
Extensible: new appenders/formatters/filters without editing the core
Optional async logging without losing/blocking on records
clarifying_questions: Which levels and what ordering? Do we need custom levels?
Sinks at launch — console, file, rotating file, network/Kafka?
Is logging synchronous or should we support async with a buffer?
Do loggers form a hierarchy (like Log4j's dotted names) with inheritance?
Do we need structured/JSON logging and contextual fields (MDC)?
How is configuration supplied — code, file, and is hot reload needed?

core_classes.name: LogRecord / LogEvent
core_classes.responsibility: Immutable value: the log message and its metadata.

core_classes.name: Logger
core_classes.responsibility: Client-facing entry point; guards on level then hands accepted records to appenders; part of the hierarchy.

core_classes.name: LoggerFactory / LogManager
core_classes.responsibility: Creates and caches named loggers; wires the hierarchy; holds config.

core_classes.name: Appender / Sink
core_classes.responsibility: Abstraction over a destination; owns a Formatter and optional Filter; writes formatted records.

core_classes.name: ConsoleAppender / FileAppender / RollingFileAppender / NetworkAppender / AsyncAppender
core_classes.responsibility: Concrete sinks; AsyncAppender wraps another appender with a queue + worker thread.

core_classes.name: Formatter / Layout
core_classes.responsibility: Strategy: turn a LogRecord into an output string.

core_classes.name: Filter
core_classes.responsibility: Chain-of-responsibility node returning ACCEPT/DENY/NEUTRAL for a record (e.g. by marker, regex, rate).

relationships: Logger composes 0..* Appenders and links to a parent Logger, forming a tree with the root at the top.
Effective level is inherited from the nearest ancestor with a configured level (Chain of Responsibility up the tree).
Appender additivity: a record accepted by a logger also goes to ancestors' appenders unless additivity is disabled.
Appender composes exactly one Formatter (Strategy) and an optional Filter chain.
LoggerFactory owns the registry and the root logger; loggers are created lazily by dotted name.

design_patterns.where: Logger hierarchy (level lookup + appender additivity up to root) and the Filter chain in an appender
design_patterns.why: A record walks up ancestors for effective level/appenders and through filters until a decision — each node handles or delegates.
Output format varies independently of destination; swap without editing the appender.

design_patterns.where: LoggerFactory/LogManager caching one Logger per name
design_patterns.why: Centralized creation and a single shared registry/config.

design_patterns.where: AsyncAppender wraps a synchronous appender with a queue/worker
design_patterns.why: Adds async behavior without changing the wrapped appender.

state_transitions: Per call: guard isEnabled(level) → build LogRecord → filter chain (ACCEPT/DENY) → format → append to each appender → propagate to ancestors if additive
AsyncAppender: record ENQUEUED → worker DEQUEUES → WRITTEN | DROPPED (queue full, drop/block policy)
Appender lifecycle: OPEN → CLOSED (flush + release resources)
edge_cases: Level below threshold → return immediately, before building the record or evaluating expensive arguments
Expensive message args (string concat) → guard with isEnabled or lazy/lambda suppliers
One appender's I/O fails → isolate so it doesn't break other appenders or the caller
Recursive logging (logging inside an appender) → guard against infinite loops
Async queue full → drop-oldest vs block vs discard, per policy
Config hot reload while logging → swap config atomically
Very high volume → batching/async to avoid blocking app threads
concurrency: Concurrent writes to a shared file/console → synchronize the write or use a single writer thread
AsyncAppender: lock-free/bounded queue + dedicated worker to keep app threads off I/O
Backpressure policy when the queue saturates (block, drop, or discard low levels)
isEnabled fast-path avoids any locking when the level is disabled
Loggers are cached and effectively immutable after configuration for lock-free reads
extensibility: New sink (Kafka, syslog, cloud) → new Appender, no Logger change
New layout (JSON, GELF) → new Formatter strategy
New filter (rate limit, sampling, marker) → new Filter node
Structured logging / MDC context propagation → fields on LogRecord
Async wrapping and batching applied by composition (Decorator)

deep_dives.probe: logger.debug("x=" + expensiveToString()) when DEBUG is disabled — the string still gets built. How does your API avoid paying that cost? Where does the level guard live?
Explain how a logger named 'com.app.svc' gets its effective level and appenders from ancestors. What is appender additivity and how do you turn it off?
Why separate Appender (where) from Formatter (how it looks)? Show adding a JSON layout to the file appender and a plain layout to console without duplicating code.
Design AsyncAppender: queue, worker, and what happens when the queue fills. Drop, block, or discard low-priority records — defend your choice.
Two threads log to the same FileAppender simultaneously. How do you keep lines from interleaving without killing throughput?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions level or debug or filter
followup_bank.question: If DEBUG is off, does logger.debug("x="+build()) still build the string? How does your design avoid that cost?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions appender or sink or file or console
followup_bank.question: Add a Kafka appender. What changes in Logger? And how do you keep one appender's failure from breaking the others?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions format or layout or json
followup_bank.question: Why is formatting separate from the appender? Show a JSON layout on file and plain on console.

followup_bank.trigger: mentions hierarchy or parent or root
followup_bank.question: How does 'com.app' inherit level and appenders from its parents, and what is additivity?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions async or queue or thread
followup_bank.question: Design the async path: what queue, what worker, and what's the policy when it's full?

tradeoffs: Synchronous (simple, ordered, blocks app) vs async (fast app threads, possible loss/reorder)
isEnabled guard / lazy suppliers (cheap when off) vs always building the record (simple, wasteful)
Per-appender lock (simple) vs single writer thread (higher throughput, more machinery)
Appender additivity on (convenient) vs off (explicit, avoids duplicate lines)
reference.reference_answer: A strong answer separates four responsibilities: Logger (whether to log, via a cheap level guard and the hierarchy), Appender (where), Formatter/Layout (how it looks, as a Strategy), and Filter (fine-grained ACCEPT/DENY as a Chain of Responsibility). Named loggers form a tree; effective level and appender additivity resolve by walking ancestors to the root — the canonical Chain-of-Responsibility. It nails the disabled-level fast path (guard before building the record / lazy suppliers) so logging is near-free when off, makes shared-sink writes thread-safe, and offers an AsyncAppender (Decorator) with an explicit queue-full policy. New sinks and layouts plug in via OCP with zero Logger changes. Signal: the fast-path cost argument and the hierarchy/additivity model.

interviewer_notes: Let them enumerate the responsibilities; the strong signal is a clean four-way split (Logger/Appender/Formatter/Filter) rather than a Logger that formats and writes. Drive the disabled-level fast path hard — 'does debug() still build the string when DEBUG is off?' separates mid from strong. Ensure Formatter is a Strategy independent of Appender (test with 'JSON on file, plain on console'). Explore the logger hierarchy and additivity as the Chain-of-Responsibility. Reserve time for thread-safety on a shared sink and the AsyncAppender queue-full policy. Test OCP with 'add a Kafka appender.'
